When the pandemic closed school buildings in 2020, millions of students suddenly learned what it meant to attend class from a kitchen table. Some thrived, many struggled, and nearly everyone formed an opinion. Now that schools can choose whether to keep distance learning as an option, the question deserves a calmer answer than the emergency allowed. I believe students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home, provided it remains an option rather than a requirement, because flexibility serves students whose needs the traditional classroom cannot meet, it builds skills they will need later, and it keeps learning going when circumstances would otherwise stop it.

The strongest reason is that students are not all alike, and a single format inevitably leaves some behind. Consider a student with a chronic illness who misses weeks of school every year. In the old system, she would fall behind and spend months catching up, often alone with a stack of photocopied worksheets. With the option to join class by video, she can hear the same explanations, ask the same questions, and stay connected to her classmates on days when she cannot leave the house. The same is true for a student who is caring for a younger sibling, recovering from surgery, or living far from school in a rural area where a bus ride takes over an hour each way. For these students, distance learning is not a convenience but the difference between participating and disappearing.

Distance learning also helps students who find the physical classroom difficult for other reasons. A shy student who never raises her hand may type a thoughtful comment into a chat window. A student who is bullied in the hallways may finally be able to concentrate on algebra instead of on avoiding certain people. These are not small advantages. Learning depends on a sense of safety and on the chance to contribute, and for some students home provides both more reliably than school does.

A second reason is that attending class from home teaches independence and self-management. Without a teacher standing at the front of the room, a student has to organize her own time, keep track of deadlines, and decide to pay attention. Critics see this as a weakness, and for some students it is. But these are exactly the skills that college and most modern jobs demand. Many adults now work remotely at least part of the week, communicate through video calls, and are trusted to finish projects without supervision. A student who has practiced these habits in high school will be better prepared than one who has only ever followed a bell schedule.

Not every family has a reliable internet connection or a quiet place to work, and screens cannot fully replace the energy of a lab experiment or a group discussion. Some students need the structure of a building and the presence of adults to stay on track. These concerns are serious, but they are arguments for doing distance learning well, not for abolishing it. Schools can lend laptops and hotspots, keep hands-on activities in person, and check in regularly with students who choose to learn from home.

Giving students the choice to attend from home does not take anything away from those who prefer the classroom. It simply opens a door for those who need it. A school's purpose is to help every student learn, and offering more than one way to show up is one of the most practical ways to fulfill that purpose.

School is more than the delivery of information, and the things that make it valuable are exactly the things that a screen tends to weaken.

The first problem is attention. At home, a student watching a video lesson is surrounded by distractions that a classroom is designed to remove. The phone is within reach, the television is in the next room, and no one notices if the camera is turned off. Even motivated students find it hard to focus on a small rectangle for six hours a day. During the school closures of 2020 and 2021, many teachers reported talking to a grid of black squares, unsure whether anyone was listening. Studies of that period found that students in many countries lost months of learning, especially in mathematics. A classroom is not a perfect environment, but it is one where a teacher can see a confused face and stop to explain again.

The second problem is that learning is social. Students learn a great deal from each other: by arguing about the meaning of a poem, by working through a chemistry problem in pairs, or simply by watching how a classmate approaches a task. A student who attends from home misses the lunch conversations, the clubs, and the hallway encounters that shape who they become.

One student has a quiet bedroom, fast internet, and parents who can help with homework. Another shares a small apartment with younger siblings, relies on a phone for internet access, and has no adult at home during the day. When both attend class from home, the gap between them grows wider. School buildings, for all their flaws, give every student the same desk, the same library, and the same teacher. Education is ultimately a human relationship between teachers and students and among students themselves. Video conferencing can support that relationship in emergencies, but it cannot replace it. For most students, the best place to learn is still a classroom full of other people.

At the time it felt kind of boring, but when school started, we jumped right into that unit and I already knew the basics. Kids who didn't do the project were lost for the first two weeks. If I had designed my own project, I would have picked something random that I liked, maybe about World War II, and it wouldn't have helped me at all in that class.

Another reason is that teachers can control how much work the project takes. When students design their own projects, some of them go way overboard and stress themselves out, while others do almost nothing. I have a friend who decided to make a full documentary for an independent project and ended up spending her whole vacation on it because she didn't realize how much work it would be. A teacher has done this many times and knows what's realistic. They can design something that takes a reasonable amount of time, like a couple hours a week, so students still get to enjoy their summer while keeping their skills fresh.

Teacher-designed projects are also easier to grade fairly. If every student does something completely different, how is a teacher supposed to compare a poster about sharks to a short story to a model volcano? The grading would end up being pretty subjective, and some students might feel like they got a worse grade just because the teacher liked another topic more. When everyone does the same assignment with the same rubric, the expectations are clear. You know what an A looks like before you even start, and that feels a lot more fair.

I know a lot of students would say that student-designed projects are more fun and more creative. I agree that choice matters, and I don't think teacher-designed has to mean boring. Teachers can build choices into their projects. They could let students pick from a few different books, choose which experiment to do, or decide whether to write an essay or make a presentation. That way students still have some control, but the project is still focused on what they actually need to learn. This is better than complete freedom, which can lead to projects that are either way too easy or way too hard.

Overall, summer projects are meant to prepare students for the next school year, and teachers are the ones who know what that preparation should look like. Teacher-designed projects connect to the real curriculum, keep the workload manageable, and give everyone a fair shot at a good grade. Students can still have some choice, but the teacher should be the one in charge of the design.

Last summer I got really into photography, and I spent hours learning about lighting and composition from online videos and practicing around my neighborhood. Nobody assigned it to me, and I still worked harder on it than on any school project. If my school had let me turn that into my summer project, maybe by writing about what I learned and showing a portfolio, it would have been real learning instead of busywork.
